read.title: No free lunch in machines
text: A lever, a pulley, a ramp, and a gear train all do the same thing: they let a small force move a large load by spreading the work over a longer distance. Work is force times distance, and a machine cannot make more work than it receives. If a lever multiplies your force by five, your hand must move five times as far as the load.

Mechanical advantage is the ratio of output force to input force. Real machines lose some energy to friction, so efficiency, useful work out divided by work in, is always below 100%. Some machines deliberately have an advantage below one. Your forearm is a third-class lever: muscle pulls near the elbow, which costs force but makes the hand move fast and far.

Rotating machines use the same logic with torque and angular speed. Power equals torque times angular velocity, P = τω, with ω in radians per second. A small gear driving one with four times as many teeth turns the output at one quarter of the speed but, ignoring losses, with four times the torque. That is why a car uses low gear to climb a hill and high gear to cruise.
